newsitem.title: USA: More women seen winning office in U.S. elections.
newsitem.headline: More women seen winning office in U.S. elections.

text.p: Women's political groups are optimistic about their chances this year, but do not expect a repeat of 1992, known as the Year of the Woman in U.S. politics when females were elected in record numbers.
"I think it'll be a good year for women, but it's not going to be 1992," former congresswoman Marjorie Margolies-Mezvinsky said in a telephone interview.

Swept into Congress along with 27 other women on the Election Day that brought Bill Clinton to the White House, Margolies-Mezvinsky was swept out again in 1994, along with eight other Democratic congresswomen. Republicans gained seven women representatives that year.

There are now 49 women in the 435-member House of Representatives. Just nine of the 100 senators are women, although that is a record number for that legislative body, and only one of the 50 states has a woman governor.

What's more, two of the most prominent women in U.S. politics -- Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas and Democratic Representative Patricia Schroeder of Colorado -- announced they would not run again in this election.

Still, Margolies-Mezvinsky believes 1996 could see breakthroughs for women in offices from the Senate to local judgeships. She is president of the Women's Campaign Fund, a non-partisan group that expects to raise some $1.5 million to help fund female candidates who favour abortion rights.
She is not alone. EMILY's List, one of the biggest political fund-raising groups for women candidates, has so far raised $6 million for Democratic office-seekers who favour abortion rights.
"I'm feeling a lot better than I was at the beginning of the year, when I thought, where are we even going to get some candidates to run?" EMILY's List spokeswoman Karin Johanson said by telephone.

Johanson said her group -- whose acronym stands for the political maxim "early money is like yeast" -- had hopes of adding 10 women into the House of Representatives, and one more woman to the Senate.

Asked to name a few races where her group has focused attention, Johanson mentioned the New Hampshire race for governor, where Democrat Jeanne Shaheen was running far ahead of Republican Ovid Lamontagne.

Another key race is the contest for Senate in Louisiana, where Mary Landrieu, who favours abortion rights, is running well against Republican Woody Jenkins, a self-described conservative who opposes abortion rights.

The Wish List, which stands for Women in the House and Senate and backs Republican women who favour abortion rights, has given out $325,000 so far to a total of 25 candidates, the group's political director, Karen Raye, said.

The Susan B. Anthony List, a non-partisan political action committee that has raised $250,000 for anti-abortion women candidates, is endorsing 12 women running for the House and one looking to join the Senate.
This group's executive director, Jennifer Bingham, was highly positive about her candidates' chances.
"I think that our candidates have a great shot," Bingham said by telephone. "Women have a great chance and the more viable ones are the ones who are pro-life."
